name: The Brown boarding-house household
head: brown_rufus

arrival.note: He is a church founder in June 1833 and a militia signatory in 1832, so the household is in the town by then; nothing dates its arrival. The 1832 militia list is the earlier evidence and this value is the conservative reading of it.

lives_at.note: Phase one recorded both links as null with the reason 'NOT MODELLED, AND IT SHOULD BE'. The building now exists and both fields point at it. Linked by the inferred-household programme's building parcel (docs/ROADMAP.md K1, phase two); the building record carries the evidence.

present_on_scene_date.note: Documented in the town in 1832 and 1833. Nothing follows the boarding house to 1835, and boarding houses in a town whose population was quadrupling are exactly the businesses that changed hands.

persons.name: Rufus Brown

occupation.note: Andreas names the house as his - 'the log house of Rufus Brown, where Mr. Porter found table board' - and names his wife as the keeper: 'Mrs. Rufus Brown kept one of the first-class boarding houses.' Which of them the trade belongs to is a question the source answers in favour of his wife and the record says so.

persons.note: One of the nine village citizens among the twenty-six founding members of the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833, and a signatory of the 1832 militia agreement submitting to Gholson Kercheval as captain 'until all apprehension of danger from the Indians may have subsided'.

refusals.reason: This card rests on 1 thing(s) the consolidation did not read — andreas_1884_v1. G2b fired on the seven domains the ladder reads and says nothing about the evidence outside them, so the grade stands. The same reasoning the ladder's own G5 gives for abstaining (T-0515).

merge_ruling.for_merge: Nothing but the strip. After it, both readings are `Rufus B Brown` letter for letter, which is M1 — and M1 firing here is the defect, not the argument.
merge_ruling.against_merge: Fergus 1843 prints them as two entries, one after the other: 458 `Brown, Rufus B., warehouse man, John P. Chapin & Co., res 189 Lake [died, Burlington, Wis., September 2, 1872, aged 69]` and 459 `Brown, Mrs. Rufus B., dress and cloak maker, 189 Lake, up stairs [died February 2, 1890, aged 73.]`. Two trades, two death notices eighteen years apart, one address — a husband and a wife at 189 Lake, and a directory does not enter one person twice under two spellings. The cards read as one person only because the splitter strips `Mrs` before it compares the names.

persons.name: Mrs Rufus Brown

occupation.note: 'Mrs. Rufus Brown kept one of the first-class boarding houses' - the trade is attributed to her in terms, in a sentence about how the town housed its transients when 'full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides'.

persons.note: A WOMAN NAMED ONLY BY HER HUSBAND'S NAME AND DOCUMENTED AS THE PROPRIETOR OF A BUSINESS, which is a combination this literature produces constantly and this schema has to be able to carry. Two women named Brown are among the nine village citizens founding the First Presbyterian Church in June 1833 - 'Mrs. Elizabeth Brown' and 'Mrs. Cynthia Brown' - and one of them may be this woman. The record does not choose: identifying her with either would manufacture a forename out of a surname.

research_note: THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THIS PARCEL WHOSE BUILDING IS DOCUMENTED, POSITIONED AND ABSENT FROM THE MODEL. Andreas gives the fabric (log), the use (first-class boarding house), the keeper (Mrs Rufus Brown) and the position (immediately behind Peck's store at South Water and LaSalle) - which is more than several buildings already standing in this scene have. A structure record for it is the highest-value single piece of work this parcel has generated. WHY BOARDING HOUSES MATTER OUT OF ALL PROPORTION TO THEIR NUMBER: Andreas says the hotels and boarding houses of 1834 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides', with emigrants living in their covered wagons outside. The gap between 3,265 people and the dwellings this dataset can name is bridged largely by buildings like this one.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
